title: Weather signs
summary: What clouds and falling or rising pressure usually mean, with the Beaufort wind scale in km/h and knots. Also lightning safety, wind chill and frostbite times, and humidex and heat index limits for heat illness.

steps.text: Look at the sky and match the cloud to the first table.
Read the pressure change over 3 hours and the wind force on the Beaufort table.
Use the lightning, wind chill and heat tables to decide when to take shelter, cover up or cool down.
steps.warn: Heat stroke and severe frostbite are emergencies. Call emergency services if you can reach them.

notes:
## Clouds

Heights: **low** below about 2,000 m (6,500 ft), **middle** to about 6,000 m (20,000 ft), **high** above that (NOAA).

| Cloud | Look | Weather link (NOAA) |
|---|---|---|
| **Cirrus** (high) | thin white wisps of ice crystals | no rain from it |
| **Cirrostratus** (high) | clear whitish veil | halo round sun or moon |
| **Altostratus** (middle) | grey or bluish sheet, sun dim | light precipitation possible |
| **Nimbostratus** (middle) | dark grey, blocks the sun | steady rain or snow |
| **Stratus** (low) | uniform grey layer | drizzle or snow grains if thick |
| **Cumulus** (low) | puffy mounds, flat base | fair weather |
| **Cumulonimbus** (low, tall) | towering, flat anvil top, dark base | thunderstorm, hail, tornado |

- A warm front brings widespread layered cloud and precipitation, so high veils thickening to grey layers and then rain fit one. A cold front brings a narrow band of showers and thunderstorms (NOAA).
- Rain mostly falls from cumulus, cumulonimbus and nimbostratus (NOAA).

## Barometer

Standard sea-level pressure is 1013.25 hPa (= mb) or 29.92 inHg (NOAA). Watch the **change over 3 hours** (Met Office).

| Change in 3 h | Called |
|---|---|
| 0.1–1.5 hPa | slowly |
| 1.6–3.5 hPa | plain "rising" or "falling" |
| 3.6–6.0 hPa | quickly |
| over 6.0 hPa | very rapidly |

- A sudden fall often means high wind. Falling when very hot: thunder. Falling in frost: thaw (NOAA).
- Rising in winter: frost. Rising and holding high after wet weather: fine within a day or two. Erratic: unsettled (NOAA).
- Changes are biggest in the northern US and Alaska. In the tropics the rules fail. Pressure also swings daily: lowest near 4 a.m. and 4 p.m., highest near 10 a.m. and 10 p.m. (NOAA).

## Beaufort wind scale

| Force | Name | km/h | Knots | On land |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Calm | under 1 | under 1 | smoke rises straight |
| 1 | Light air | 1–5 | 1–3 | smoke drifts |
| 2 | Light breeze | 6–11 | 4–6 | felt on face, leaves rustle |
| 3 | Gentle breeze | 12–19 | 7–10 | twigs in motion |
| 4 | Moderate | 20–28 | 11–16 | dust, loose paper lifts |
| 5 | Fresh | 29–38 | 17–21 | small trees sway |
| 6 | Strong | 39–49 | 22–27 | large branches move |
| 7 | Near gale | 50–61 | 28–33 | whole trees move; hard to walk |
| 8 | Gale | 62–74 | 34–40 | twigs break; progress blocked |
| 9 | Severe gale | 75–88 | 41–47 | slight structural damage |
| 10 | Storm | 89–102 | 48–55 | trees uprooted |
| 11 | Violent storm | 103–117 | 56–63 | widespread damage |
| 12 | Hurricane | 118–133 | 64–71 | severe damage |

Sources: ECCC (speeds), NWS (names).

## Lightning

- **Count flash to bang.** Seconds divided by 3 = km (by 5 = miles) (NWS).
- **30-30 rule:** under 30 s between flash and thunder means take shelter at once. Stay in until 30 min after the last thunder (ECCC via WorkSafeNB; NWS).
- If you can hear thunder, you are within striking distance. Lightning often hits more than 5 km from the storm centre, and bolts from the blue can land 16–24 km away (NWS).
- **Safe:** a proper building, or a closed vehicle with a metal roof (NWS, ECCC). Convertibles, golf carts and tractors are not safe (NWS).
- **Not safe:** open fields, hilltops, ridges, tall lone trees, water, metal fences and poles, tents, picnic shelters, sheds, dugouts (NWS). Do not lie flat.
- Camping in the open: pitch in a valley or low ground. In a group, spread out (NWS).

## Wind chill (ECCC)

| Wind chill | Risk | Exposed skin can freeze in |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to −9 | low | discomfort |
| −10 to −27 | moderate | long exposure risks frostbite and hypothermia |
| −28 to −39 | high | 10–30 min |
| −40 to −47 | very high | 5–10 min |
| −48 to −54 | severe | 2–5 min |
| −55 or colder | extreme | under 2 min |

- Faster in sustained wind over 50 km/h (ECCC).
- Example: −20 °C with 30 km/h wind feels like −33 (ECCC).
- US chart: frostbite in 30 min at about −19 °F (−28 °C) (NWS).
- Frostbite needs air below 0 °C. Hypothermia is a core temperature under 35 °C (NOAA).

## Heat

**Humidex** (ECCC): 20–29 little discomfort. 30–39 some discomfort. 40–45 great discomfort, avoid exertion. 46 and over dangerous, possible heat stroke.

**Heat index** (NWS, shade values; full sun adds up to 8 °C):

| Heat index | Effect with long exposure or hard work |
|---|---|
| 27–32 °C (80–90 °F) | fatigue possible |
| 32–39 °C (90–103 °F) | cramps, exhaustion, heat stroke possible |
| 39–51 °C (103–124 °F) | cramps or exhaustion likely, heat stroke possible |
| 52 °C+ (125 °F+) | heat stroke highly likely |

Some NWS offices use 105 and 130 °F as the cut-offs.

**Heat exhaustion** (CDC): heavy sweating, cold pale clammy skin, fast weak pulse, nausea, cramps, dizziness, fainting. Move to a cool place, loosen clothes, apply cool wet cloths, sip water. Get medical help if vomiting, worse, or not better in 1 hour.

**Heat stroke** (CDC): body temperature 39.4 °C (103 °F) or higher, hot red dry or damp skin, fast strong pulse, confusion, passing out. **Call emergency services (911) right away** if you can reach them. If not, see [When no help is coming](#ref/reference_weather/when_no_help_is_coming). Cool with wet cloths or a cool bath. Give nothing to drink.

On hot days avoid hiking from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. (USFS). Never leave a child or pet in a parked car (NWS).

## When no help is coming

**Heat stroke** (confusion, collapse, hot skin)
- Cool at once, before anything else. Best is whole-body immersion in ice water, or the coldest water you have (WMS heat). Neck down in water from 1 to 26 °C works, and colder is faster (ILCOR).
- Keep the head clear of the water and protect the airway (OutdoorEd).
- No bath: loosen or remove clothes, keep the skin wet with cold water and fan hard. This is about half as fast (WMS heat).
- Ice packs: cover the whole body. With only a few, use cheeks, palms and soles (WMS heat).
- Do not delay cooling to give drinks (WMS heat).
- Stop at a core temperature of about 38.3 to 38.8 °C (WMS heat). With no thermometer, cool until thinking clears. ILCOR gives 15 minutes as a reasonable time, not a limit: if still confused, keep cooling (ILCOR).
- After: watch breathing and alertness. Confusion, seizures or no sweating are danger signs (St John NSW). A previously healthy person back to normal within two hours can recover under watch. Heat stroke without exertion, as in older or ill people, needs a higher level of care even if cooling works (WMS heat).

**Severe frostbite** (hard, waxy, numb skin)
- Treat hypothermia and serious injury first (WMS frostbite).
- If it could refreeze, do not thaw it. Keep it frozen until it can stay thawed. Avoid walking on a thawed foot (WMS frostbite).
- If it can stay thawed, rewarm in a 37 to 39 °C water bath for about 30 minutes, until red or purple and soft. With no thermometer, the water should feel tolerable on a helper's uninjured hand for 30 seconds. No fire or hot rocks (WMS frostbite, AAFP).
- If you cannot keep up a bath, let it thaw alone or by body heat in a warm shelter (WMS frostbite).
- Do not rub. Air dry or blot. Leave blisters alone, and never drain blood-filled ones (WMS frostbite).
- Dress with dry bulky gauze, wrapped loosely for swelling. Raise it above the heart (WMS frostbite).
